intro_en: The Israel National Trail crosses Yatir Forest, the largest planted forest in Israel, and climbs up Har Amasa, one of the highest points along the entire trail. Along the way we briefly leave the Negev for its neighbour to the north, the Hebron Hills.
character_en: (For those walking north to south) A gentle climb for most of the length of the segment. Large parts pass through the forest, but there are also exposed sections. Several forest picnic areas with tables along the trail.
transport_en: The entrance to Meitar. The community of Har Amasa (infrequent service)
pois_en: An ancient water cistern. Mitzpe Noam. Horvat Yatir (lookout point). Sternbergia flowering (in November). The community of Har Amasa.
important_en: There is a water tap beside the gate of the Forester's House (Beit HaYa'aran); to get in you need to ask the guard.
There are pits and caves alongside the trail.
Har Amasa is higher than Jerusalem. On winter days with a strong wind it can be very cold, and with a little luck there may even be snow.
description_en:
We start walking from the eastern side of the Devambam Bridge, named after Gershon Dubinbaum, who was killed in this area in the War of Independence in October 1948 (see the Wikipedia entry for more).
The trail advances along a blue-marked road, a scenic road that continues east into Yatir Forest as far as the Forester's House. The road climbs the nearby ridge, and at its highest point turns right along the crest of the ridge. At this point the Israel National Trail continues straight on between the pine trees, "cutting" a bend made by the vehicle road, descends in a straight line and rejoins the vehicle road in the gully.
We advance a short distance further along the vehicle road, as far as a forest picnic area with tables and a water tap. At the corner of the picnic area, the trail turns right onto a dirt road, crosses a ridge and descends into a wide gully. On the other side of the gully, the trail enters a small gully between pine trees, with a forest picnic area with tables ahead of us and, on the left, on an earth embankment, a sign reading "Open Pit". The sign marks the location of an ancient water cistern; it is worth approaching carefully to take a look.
The trail continues up the ridge, and after a few minutes of climbing we reach an abandoned foresters' tower on the right. Beside the tower, at the high point, there is another picnic area with tables and next to it a memorial in the shape of a piano to Noam Rosenthal, a soldier from Meitar who was killed in Operation Protective Edge.
We continue with the trail, and after a short descent and a left turn onto a dirt road, we reach the northern edge of Meitar Forest. The trail reaches a gully, the boundary line between the planted area and the bare terrain, climbs north-east up a ridge, and then meets and parts from a white, blue-marked dirt road.
After about 20 minutes of walking, we reach a saddle together with the white road. To the left we can see the security road running alongside the separation fence. At this point the trail leaves the white road and turns right onto a secondary dirt road.
The road crosses the channel of Nahal Eshtemoa and climbs north-east to the Har Hiran ridge. We reach the high summit at spot height 599. Even from afar we can identify a tall antenna to the right of the summit. At the summit, the trail turns east (right) and advances along the edge of the forest (trees on the left, bare hills on the right).
This is Hiran Forest, a north-western extension of the great Yatir Forest. From here to the end of the segment we walk through the forest or along its edges. After about 2 km, the trail crosses a narrow road that leads to a fine lookout point, the spot where the Nahal Yatir outpost settlement stood around the year 2000.
The Israel National Trail turns right and advances along the edge of the road for a short distance. At the point where the road turns sharply right, the trail turns left and descends along a dirt road, with a dome-shaped hill topped by a ruin visible on the left: Horvat Yatir. This is a fine antiquities site with a pleasant lookout at its top, but it has no marked trail and care must be taken to avoid pits.
At the meeting with a graded road, we turn right onto the road, with pine forest on the left and low trees on the right, among them Atlantic pistachio (terebinth) trees, pistachio trees planted in the 1960s in several plots within Yatir Forest.
The trail continues for about 2 km along the graded road (also marked with blue trail marking). At a sharp bend, the trail leaves the road to the right and continues to circle a bare hill visible to the right of the trail.
After a short walk, we cross a gully planted with low trees and climb a ridge leading to the "Forester's House" (Beit HaYa'aran), a KKL-JNF compound in the heart of Yatir Forest. Hikers can fill up with water at the entrance gate to the compound; you need to ask the guard to let you in.
After crossing Road 316, the road from Hura to Susya, the trail advances east along forest roads for about 7 km. About half a kilometre south of the community of Har Amasa, on the eastern edge of Yatir Forest, the segment ends. On the left we see the community of Har Amasa. At the time of writing, a new neighbourhood is being built between the Israel National Trail and the older part of the community, and the trail passes to the south, differently from the marking shown on old maps.
It is worth going in to get to know the community of Har Amasa. It is advisable to arrange in advance regarding the hikers' room (Hadar HaShvilistim) in the community.
nearby_en: The synagogue at Horvat Anim. The dwelling caves and the agricultural installations trail south of the community of Shani (Livne). The Yatir Forest Reservoir lookout, about 200 metres north of the Israel National Trail, also accessible to any vehicle by driving along the "blue" vehicle road.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel.
